title: Geopolitical energy disruption is transmitting through inflation, supply chains, household purchasing power, and developing-country fiscal space
source_unit: United Nations DESA, World Economic Situation and Prospects as of mid-2026
geography: Global economy with developed, developing, regional, and vulnerable-country outlooks

observations.period: 2026-2027; global growth and inflation outlook after the mid-2026 energy shock

global_growth_2026.unit: percent projected global GDP growth in 2026

global_growth_2027.unit: percent projected global GDP growth in 2027

observations.method: UN DESA Global Economic Monitoring Branch update using the World Economic Forecasting Model, revised after the energy and supply-chain shock.
observations.uncertainty: The forecast depends heavily on the duration and scale of the conflict, energy-market disruption, commodity prices, policy responses, and financial conditions; a faster resolution and a prolonged disruption imply materially different paths.
observations.subgroup: Global economy, developed and developing economies, households, firms, governments, and regions with different exposure to energy, food, trade, and financing shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate growth can remain positive while households face falling real purchasing power, firms face higher costs, or vulnerable countries lose development capacity; growth is not a welfare measure by itself.

observations.period: 2026; energy, freight, fertilizer, food, and supply-chain transmission

denominator.unit: global energy and supply-chain shock transmission frame

energy_route.value: constrained energy supply and closure of a major transit route

transit_share.unit: approximately percent of global oil and LNG supplies normally passing through the Strait of Hormuz

cost_channels.value: fuel, fertilizer, food, freight, insurance, transport, and import costs

food_energy_burden.value: low-income households bear the heaviest burden because food and energy take a larger share of their budgets

observations.method: UN DESA analysis of energy-market disruption, transit exposure, commodity prices, supply chains, import costs, and household purchasing-power channels.
observations.uncertainty: The scale and persistence of pass-through depend on inventories, substitution, market structure, policy support, transport rerouting, and the conflict's duration; the report does not estimate every household's realized incidence.
observations.subgroup: Food- and fuel-importing developing economies, low-income households, energy-intensive firms, transport and logistics systems, and populations exposed to food insecurity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some producers and energy companies may receive windfall gains, while subsidies, stockpiles, alternative routes, or targeted support can buffer pass-through for particular places or groups.

observations.period: 2026; fiscal, financial, labour, and development-capacity consequences

denominator.unit: global public-capacity and development-finance response frame

external_finance.value: tighter external financing conditions and possible portfolio outflows

fiscal_pressure.value: weaker growth plus crisis-cushioning expenditures increase fiscal pressure

policy_dilemma.value: higher rates may contain inflation while weakening growth; holding rates may entrench price pressure

development_risk.value: food insecurity, poverty, debt vulnerability, and slower SDG progress

observations.method: UN DESA synthesis of monetary, fiscal, trade, labour, industrial, financial, and international-cooperation channels.
observations.uncertainty: These are forecast mechanisms and risks, not measured causal effects or uniform country outcomes; policy choices and international coordination can alter the path.
observations.subgroup: Developing-country governments, central banks, workers, firms, households, lenders, aid recipients, and populations already facing debt or food insecurity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Resilient labour markets, consumer demand, AI-related investment, fiscal support, and international coordination may offset part of the shock, but their benefits can be unevenly distributed.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical-shock-to-energy, inflation, supply-chain, household-purchasing-power, financial, fiscal, and development-capacity route. It is not household-level incidence data, a price pass-through estimate for a specific product, a causal geopolitical evaluation, or proof of realized poverty, political action, or state failure.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN DESA publication page and mid-year PDF were retrieved; growth, inflation, Strait of Hormuz exposure, household purchasing-power, financing, fiscal, and development-risk claims were cross-checked against the report summary and PDF sections.
